# PROPPS PTY LTD - full content

> PROPPS PTY LTD is Australia's premier provider of cinema-grade reproduction currency and prop cash, engineered strictly in compliance with Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 Section 22 guidelines for film, television, theatre, advertising, and simulation arts.

- Products are non-legal tender reproduction props for film, television, theatre, photography and training. Every note carries specimen markings (Crimes (Currency) Act 1981, Section 22).

- Dispatch by Australia Post Express with signature on delivery.

## Frequently asked questions
### Is prop money legal to buy and use in Australia?
Yes. Prop currency is completely legal to purchase and use in Australia for legitimate motion picture, television, theatrical, commercial, and training productions provided it adheres to the Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 and Reserve Bank of Australia reproduction guidelines, featuring prominent non-negotiable reproduction markings.

### Can this prop money be spent or circulated as legal tender?
Absolutely not. PROPPS PTY LTD reproduction currency is strictly non-legal tender. Attempting to spend, circulate, or deceive any person or machine with prop currency is a severe criminal offence under Commonwealth law carrying substantial prison penalties.

### What materials are used for your Australian prop banknotes?
Our prop currency is printed on specialized 120gsm high-grade matte archival paper rather than polymer film. This matte finish prevents studio camera reflections, handles realistically during counting scenes, and ensures clear distinction from genuine legal currency.

### What is the minimum order requirement and shipping cost?
Our minimum order value is $300 AUD. Orders of $500 AUD and above qualify for free Australia-wide express shipping. Orders below $500 incur a flat $20 AUD Australia Post Express shipping fee with mandatory signature on delivery.

### How does the 10% cryptocurrency discount work?
When selecting cryptocurrency payment (Bitcoin, USDT TRC20, or Ethereum), a 10% discount is automatically deducted from your order subtotal. You will receive transfer instructions and can confirm your transaction with a TXID.

### Do you offer bulk wholesale pricing for film production studios?
Yes. We supply major streaming studios, theatre companies, escape rooms, and financial training institutions across Australia with custom bulk quantities, specialised serial numbers, and custom vault bricks with tiered wholesale discounts.

### Where are you based and how fast is dispatch?
We are based in Melbourne, Victoria (Eltham, VIC 3093). All orders are packaged discreetly in tamper-evident security boxes and dispatched via Express Australia Post within 24 business hours of payment confirmation.

### Realistic Fake Money Australia: 5 Pro Photography Tips
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/realistic-fake-money-australia-photography-tips/
- Published: 2026-10-12

When arranging your prop money australia, fanning the notes manually creates a more organic look than a perfect machine-stacked pile. For a high-impact shot, placing a prop $100 australia note in the foreground can lead the viewer's eye. Our au prop money is specifically engineered for these types of high-resolution shoots, ensuring your prop money aud looks authentic even in the tightest of close-ups.

For stills, set the notes on a matte surface and light from the side rather than straight on, which keeps the paper from throwing a hot spot. Shoot a few frames with the notes slightly fanned so the print detail on both sides shows. If the notes will appear in an advertisement, keep the specimen markings visible in at least one frame so the image stays on the right side of the Crimes (Currency) Act.

### Prop Money for Music Videos in Australia: What Works on Camera
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/prop-money-for-music-videos-australia/
- Published: 2026-10-11

Prop money for music videos has to look good fast. Shoots are short, framing is tight and notes are often thrown, fanned or held to camera.

What tends to work:
1. Double-sided notes that survive being flipped and fanned.
2. Matte paper that avoids glare under LED and strobe lighting.
3. Loose notes plus one stack, so there is enough to throw without running out.

Keep the markings visible and never hand notes to the public as real money. For stills and clips, our [photography range](/shop/photography-props/) is the place to start.

Because music video shoots are fast and often outdoors, take care with handling: notes thrown into the air or fanned in front of a fan will spread quickly, so brief the crew to collect them between takes. Keep a spare set for the hero shot, and avoid handing notes to members of the public as props in a public location, where someone could mistake them for real money.

### Double-Sided Prop Banknotes (AUD): Why Both Sides Matter on Set
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/double-sided-prop-banknotes-aud-why-both-sides-matter/
- Published: 2026-10-11

Double-sided prop banknotes cost slightly more to make, and they pay for themselves the first time a note is flipped on camera.

Where both sides matter:
- Counting scenes, where the back is visible as notes are fanned.
- Handoffs, where a note is turned over in a hand.
- Close-ups at 4K, where a blank back is obvious.

PROPPS notes are printed on both sides in high definition and carry specimen markings throughout. See the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) for every denomination.

Double-sided printing also helps with continuity. When an actor turns a note over between takes, the back should match from one take to the next, and a printed reverse makes that automatic. It is a small detail, but it is one of the first things a close-up or a freeze-frame exposes, and it is the difference between a note that reads as real on screen and one that does not.

### The Art Department's Guide to Australian Prop Money Realistic Aging
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/art-departments-guide-prop-money-aging/
- Published: 2026-10-10

A brand new, crisp australian prop money realistic stack can sometimes look too perfect for a gritty underworld scene. Art departments often need their prop money au to look like it has been "around the block." While we offer pre-distressed bundles, achieving your own custom aging for au prop money can be done with a few professional secrets.

One common technique is the "hand-roll"—gently rolling individual australian prop money notes in your palms to break the paper's stiffness without creating sharp creases. For a stained look, a very light misting of tea or coffee can add a subtle yellowing to a fake note australia, though this must be done sparingly to avoid soaking the archival paper. Our aus prop money is designed to take these modifications well, allowing your team to create the exact level of wear needed for the character's backstory. Remember to always keep a few pristine realistic fake money australia notes for "mint condition" shots.

### Ready Prop Money: Stacks That Arrive Set-Ready for Fast Turnarounds
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/ready-prop-money-stacks-for-fast-turnaround/
- Published: 2026-10-10

Call sheets change. A scene moves a day earlier, a table spread becomes a vault reveal, or the director adds a second take of a handover with a different bag. When cash is in the shot, the art department is the department that feels it first. Ready prop money, meaning stacks that are already counted, strapped and sized, takes the preparation out of a late change. This guide explains what ready stacks are, when they save time, how to size and store them, and how to order them for a fast turnaround. Every note we sell is a specimen-marked, non-legal tender prop.

## The short answer

Ready prop money is supplied as pre-counted, strapped stacks, so the art department can place them instead of building them. It saves prep hours, keeps stacks matching across set-ups and makes late changes manageable. Orders dispatch from our Melbourne studio by Australia Post Express, with a signature required on delivery. Browse the [Money Stacks category](/shop/money-stacks/) to see what is available.

## What ready stacks are

A ready stack is a bundle of notes that has been counted and strapped at the studio. The art department opens the box, checks the count and places the stack. Nothing needs to be banded, squared or counted on the morning of the shoot. Stack sizes are standard, so you can plan around them. Our stack tiers run from a Starter Stack through 1, 5, 10, 50 and 100 stacks, which covers anything from a wallet shot to a full vault.

## Why ready stacks help on a tight schedule

1. Less prep. There is no counting or banding on the day. A prop master with a small team can dress a scene in minutes instead of an hour.
2. Consistent look. Matching stacks make continuity simpler between takes and between set-ups.
3. Fewer mistakes. A strapped stack has a known count, so you can track it in and out at the end of the day.
4. Easier handover. The second unit or a new art department assistant can pick up the stacks and place them without a briefing.
5. Faster dispatch. Orders leave our Melbourne studio by Express Post within 24 business hours of payment.

## When ready stacks matter most

Ready stacks pay off whenever time is the scarcest resource:

- Late scene changes. A move from a table spread to a vault reveal needs more stacks, not more preparation.
- Multi-camera days. Two cameras and three set-ups need identical stacks in several places at once.
- Series work. Episode six has to match episode one. Order once, and use the same size and strapping throughout.
- Small crews. Student films and independent productions rarely have a spare person to count and band notes.
- Photography. A studio shoot with an hourly rate benefits from stacks that go straight on the set.

For a longer look at how to match volume to scene, read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/) and [prop cash for heist and bank scenes](/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/).

## How to size a ready-stack order

Use a simple process:

1. Count the visible stacks. Walk the shot list and count how many stacks the camera sees in each scene.
2. Add the hidden ones. Add stacks that sit behind hero bundles, under bags or in the background. The lens may blur them, but they still need to be there.
3. Allow for continuity. If the same money appears twice in a scene, double the count for the second set-up.
4. Add a reserve. Keep one stack unopened as a spare for late changes.
5. Round up to the nearest tier. The tiers are Starter ($115), 1 Stack ($200), 5 Stacks ($850), 10 Stacks ($1,600), 50 Stacks ($7,500) and 100 Stacks ($14,000), in AUD.

Orders start at $300 AUD, delivery is free from $500 AUD and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount. For larger or repeat runs, ask about wholesale rates on our [wholesale page](/wholesale/).

## Choosing denominations for ready stacks

Ready stacks work best when the denomination mix fits the scene. Use $100 and $50 notes on the visible faces of hero stacks, because those colours read strongly on camera. Add $20, $10 and $5 stacks for tills, wallets and counters. See our [$100 bundle size guide](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/) for how to size the biggest stacks, and the guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) for the mix.

## A worked example: a three-day shoot

Imagine a short drama with a bank scene on day one, a car handover on day two and a kitchen-table scene on day three, all using the same money. The art department needs hero stacks for the bank counter, a bag for the car and a close-up bundle for the table.

With ready stacks the plan is simple. Order 5 Stacks for the bank counter and drawer, add a 1 Stack and a Starter Stack for the handover and the table, and keep one stack sealed as a reserve. Because every stack is strapped and counted, the prop master can reset the bag between takes in a minute, track the count at wrap each day and hand the same stacks to the next location. Without ready stacks, each of those resets means banding, squaring and counting by hand while the crew waits.

## Common mistakes with ready stacks

- Opening everything on day one. Keep the reserve sealed until it is needed.
- Ordering different sizes for the same scene. Matching stacks protect continuity, so keep sizes consistent across a scene.
- Not counting at wrap. A quick count at the end of the day is the cheapest way to avoid a missing-stack surprise.
- Leaving the notes unattended. Assign one person and a secure place before the parcel arrives.
- Waiting until the night before. Ready stacks are fast, but a signature is required on delivery and weekends and remote addresses take longer.

## Storing and handling ready stacks on set

A stack that is ready to place should stay that way. A few simple rules keep the notes in good shape and keep the paperwork clean:

- Keep them in the box until the scene. A strap protects the edges and keeps the count.
- Assign one person. The prop master or art department assistant is responsible for the notes, in and out, each day.
- Count at wrap. A quick count at the end of the day catches anything missing before it leaves the location.
- Keep one stack sealed. A reserve for late changes is cheaper than a rush order.
- Protect from moisture and heat. Archival paper handles normally, but damp conditions and hot cars curl edges.
- Never leave notes in a car or on a location overnight. Store them securely.

Ready stacks are still props. Every note carries permanent specimen markings, and every product is a non-legal tender reproduction made for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. They must never be spent, handed out as gifts or tips, or presented as real cash. Keep the invoice on the production file, control the notes on set and brief the cast and crew. ### 100 Dollar Prop Money: Which Bundle Size Suits Which Scene
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/
- Published: 2026-10-09

For most Australian productions, 100 dollar prop money does the heavy lifting. The denomination reads clearly on camera, signals value at a glance and holds its colour under both natural and studio light. The harder question is how much to order. Too little and the scene looks thin. Too much and the budget goes on bundles the lens never sees. This guide shows how to pick a bundle size for wallet shots, desk spreads, bag reveals and vault scenes, with the real stack sizes and prices, and a few tricks that let a small order read as a large one. All our notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Match the stack size to what the camera actually sees. A hand or wallet shot needs a Starter Stack. A desk or table spread needs one or two stacks. A bag or briefcase scene needs five. A vault or heist reveal needs ten or more, and a full bank vault scene is where 50 and 100 stack orders come in. Use hero stacks of $100 notes where the camera is close, and fill the rest of the frame with cheaper material.

## The bundle sizes and what they cost

Every product in the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) is sold in the same stack tiers. Stack sizes are described by face value, and prices are in AUD:

- Starter Stack: $1,500 face value, $115
- 1 Stack: $2,000 face value, $200
- 5 Stacks: $10,000 face value, $850
- 10 Stacks: $20,000 face value, $1,600
- 50 Stacks: $100,000 face value, $7,500
- 100 Stacks: $200,000 face value, $14,000

Orders start at $300 AUD, so a Starter Stack on its own does not clear the minimum. A Starter Stack plus a 1 Stack, or a single 5 Stacks order, is the usual way to start. Delivery is free from $500 AUD, and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount. You can see the current prices on the [$100 product page](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/).

## Match the bundle to the shot

### Wallet or hand shot

A close shot of a hand counting notes or a wallet opening only shows a few notes. One Starter Stack covers it, with plenty left over for continuity. Spend the saved budget on a clean, uncreased hero note that you keep for the close-up.

### Table spread or desk scene

A pile on a table, a desk or a car bonnet needs volume without depth. One or two stacks give a natural-looking spread. Let the notes fall loosely and vary the angles. A neat grid looks staged.

### Bag, briefcase or handover

A handover scene shows a bag opening and a thick bundle at the top. Five stacks usually fill a briefcase to the lip. Put $100 notes on top of the bundles that show, and place filler underneath. If the scene shows the same bag twice, order enough matching stacks so you are not rebuilding them between set-ups.

### Heist or vault reveal

A vault, a safe or a cash room is where the camera pulls back. This is where 10 stacks and above come in. Count the shelves, the pallets and the bags in the frame, then work out how many bundles each one holds. For the biggest scenes our [Money Stacks category](/shop/money-stacks/) and [wholesale page](/wholesale/) are the right place to start. Our guide to [prop cash for heist and bank scenes](/blog/prop-cash-for-heist-and-bank-scenes-getting-the-volume-right/) goes through the maths in detail.

## Make a small order look big

Art departments rarely buy a full vault of hero notes. These are the usual tricks:

1. Hero on top, filler underneath. The camera sees the top note and the stack edges. Put $100 notes at the visible faces and cheaper material behind them.
2. Fan the notes. A fanned handful reads as a thicker stack than a flat one.
3. Vary the denominations. An all-$100 drawer looks wrong. Mix in $50 and $20 notes, as our guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) explains.
4. Use depth of field. A shallow focus blurs bundles in the background, so you do not need hero quality there.
5. Break the line. Open a strap, spill a few notes and leave one stack at an angle. Perfect order looks fake.
6. Keep spares. Hold one stack unopened as a reserve for late changes.

## Continuity and re-takes

Continuity is the quiet cost of a cash scene. If the same money appears before and after a handover, you need matching stacks for both sides of the cut. Notes are double-sided, so a flipped stack still looks right. Order the full quantity for a block of shooting in one go, so the notes in scene 12 match the notes in scene 3. If you need a repeat order, [contact the studio](/contact/) and mention the earlier order.

## Worked examples

These three examples show how the same tiers stretch across different scenes. Quantities are a starting point. Always count what your own shot list shows.

### A bank counter scene

The camera starts on a teller counting a bundle, then cuts to a wide of the counter with a few stacks. One 5 Stacks order covers the hero stacks, the teller's drawer and a reserve. Put $100 and $50 notes on the visible faces of the bundles and use $20 and $10 notes in the drawer. Total: $850, which also clears the order minimum and delivery threshold.

### A kitchen-table handover

A character slides a bundle across a table, and the camera holds on the money for two seconds. One stack in a close-up is enough, and a Starter Stack plus a 1 Stack ($315 together) clears the minimum with room for a second take and a reserve. If the scene is shot twice from different angles, the second stack lets the art department reset instantly without rebuilding the first.

### A vault reveal

A heist or security scene pulls back to show shelves of bundles. A 10 Stacks order ($1,600) fills a modest vault. A larger set with pallets and open bags suits 50 Stacks ($7,500). A full cash room is where 100 Stacks ($14,000) and a wholesale conversation make sense. In every case, put hero stacks at the front and let depth of field handle the back.

## Common mistakes with bundle sizes

- Ordering for the whole frame instead of the visible faces. The camera sees the top of a stack, not its core.
- Forgetting the second set-up. Matching stacks for a second angle save more time than they cost.
- Buying only $100 notes. A drawer or wallet with a single denomination looks staged.
- No reserve. A single unopened stack is cheaper than a rush order on the morning of the shoot.
- Leaving it late. Express dispatch is fast, but it needs someone at the address to sign.

The Reserve Bank's current $100 note is a strong, saturated green that reads on camera under most lighting, and the denomination signals value instantly. That is why productions lean on $100 and $50 notes for hero stacks and use $20, $10 and $5 notes for tills, wallets and counters. Keep the notes with the prop master, count them in and out each day, keep the invoice on file and never spend them or hand them out. ### High Quality Prop Money: How to Judge It Before Your Shoot
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/high-quality-prop-money-how-to-judge-it-on-camera/
- Published: 2026-10-07

High quality prop money is easy to spot once you know what to look for, and just as easy to miss if you judge it from a product photo. A render can hide soft print, glare-prone paper and edges that curl after two takes. This guide gives you a practical way to judge prop money before your shoot: four checks for the notes themselves, tests you can run under your own lights, questions to put to a supplier and the red flags that tell you to walk away. It is written for art departments, photographers and directors. All PROPPS notes are specimen-marked, non-legal tender props.

## The short answer

Judge prop money on four things: print detail, paper, double-sided finish and handling. Then test a sample under the lighting you will actually use, both at arm's length and up close. Quality is not about looking identical to a real banknote. It is about reading correctly on camera while staying clearly marked and different in the hand.

## Check 1: Print detail

Fine line work is the first thing to fail in a cheap print. Hold a note at arm's length: the main design, portrait and colour blocks should look clean. Then bring it close: fine lines should stay crisp rather than turning into a blur or showing visible dots. If you are shooting a close-up of a hand counting notes, the lens will see the fine detail. If the print softens at your working distance, it will soften on camera.

Look at colour as well as detail. Saturated colourways such as the gold of the $50 and the green of the $100 should read as deep, even colours, not flat or patchy. Check that the colours match across a stack, because two print runs that do not match are a continuity problem.

## Check 2: Paper

Paper decides how a note behaves under lights. A glossy or reflective stock throws hot spots into the lens, and a thin stock looks flimsy as soon as an actor handles it. Matte, non-reflective stock handles naturally and avoids glare under studio lighting. PROPPS notes are printed on 120gsm archival paper, which is heavy enough to feel like a note and matte enough to stay out of trouble with a lighting rig. Our guide to [lighting prop money on camera without glare](/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/) goes through the lighting side.

Paper also matters for compliance. Genuine Australian banknotes are polymer, so a reproduction on paper is easy to tell apart by touch. That is a deliberate feature, not a compromise.

## Check 3: Both sides

Many cheap prints are one-sided or have a rough reverse. That matters whenever an actor fans, flips or counts notes, because the camera will see the back. Check that both sides carry the same print quality, and that the reverse is aligned with the front. Our notes are printed double-sided, so a fanned or flipped stack looks right.

## Check 4: Handling

A scene may need ten takes. Notes should survive repeated handling without curling, creasing badly or tearing. Test a sample note by folding it once, fanning it and counting it through your fingers a dozen times. Look at the corners and edges. If the corners round off or the edges fray in a few minutes, the notes will not last a day on set.

## A simple on-set test

Before you commit to a large order, run this five-minute test with a sample:

1. Light it as you will shoot it. Use your actual key light, practicals and any bounce.
2. Check at working distance. View the note through the lens or monitor at the distance of your wide, medium and close shots.
3. Tilt it. Rotate the note slowly and watch for hot spots and reflections.
4. Handle it. Fan, flip, count and fold it a dozen times.
5. Compare to your other props. Put it next to the wallet, the bag or the desk it will sit on.
6. Take photos on the camera you will use. The monitor lies less than a product page does.

## Questions to ask a supplier

Good suppliers answer these directly. Evasive answers are a warning.

1. Can I see a close-up photo of an actual note, front and back?
2. What is the paper stock and weight?
3. Are the notes printed on both sides?
4. Are the specimen markings permanent, and where are they?
5. Can I order a sample or see a hand-held video?
6. How are the notes counted and strapped?
7. Do I get an invoice and written product description for the production file?
8. How is the order delivered, and is a signature required?

## Red flags

Quality and honesty tend to travel together. Walk away if you see:

- Renders instead of photos. If every image is a mock-up, the real product may not match.
- No specimen markings. Unmarked notes are the biggest risk for buyers.
- Claims of undetectable quality or passing tests. That is the wrong promise for a prop.
- Government clearance claims with no source. Regulators do not approve individual prop sellers.
- Unmarked or discreet packaging as a selling point. Legitimate props do not need to hide.
- No Australian business details. You should be able to see an ABN and an address.

For more on weighing up suppliers, read [where to buy prop money in Australia legally](/blog/where-to-buy-prop-money-in-australia-legally/) and [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/).

## What quality means for different shoots

The same note is judged differently depending on the job:

- A feature film close-up needs crisp fine detail, accurate colour and a natural feel in the actor's hand. Judge the note at working distance and check both sides.
- A television drama often shoots fast with multiple set-ups, so handling and matching stacks matter as much as print detail.
- Theatre is viewed from a distance, so colour and durability matter more than the finest line work. Notes get handled every night.
- Photography shows everything at high resolution and under controlled lighting, so paper finish and glare control matter most. Read our [photography guide](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/).
- Content creators shoot on phones and small cameras, where bright, saturated colour and clear markings read well. See the [guide for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/).

## Keeping prop money in good condition

Even good notes can be ruined by poor storage. Keep them flat, dry and out of direct sun. Avoid leaving them in a hot car, where edges curl. Keep them strapped and in the box until the scene. Handle them by the edges, and keep a few spare notes for hero shots so the best ones are not handled more than needed. At wrap, count the notes in and store them with the prop master, never loose in a bag or costume.

## Quality is not the same as cost

A higher price does not guarantee quality, and a low price does not always mean poor quality. What matters is whether the price covers the things you cannot see on a product page: paper weight, double-sided alignment, consistent colour between runs, counting and strapping, paperwork and delivery. Our guide to [cheap prop money and what you are really paying for](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) goes through the trade-offs. At PROPPS, orders start at $300 AUD, delivery is free from $500 AUD and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount.

## Match quality to the shot

Not every shot needs the same level of detail. A close-up of a hand counting notes needs hero-quality print and handling. A wide of a vault needs volume, and a shallow depth of field will blur the bundles at the back. Put your best notes where the camera is close and use stacks for the rest. Our guide to [$100 prop money bundle sizes](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/) shows how to split an order between hero and background stacks.

## Compliance still matters

High quality does not mean realistic enough to deceive. Every note we sell carries permanent specimen markings, is printed on paper rather than polymer and is sold as a non-legal tender prop for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. Keep the notes under the prop master's control, never spend them and never post unmarked close-ups that suggest the cash is real. Read the [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and visit the [compliance page](/compliance/) for the full standard.

### Is It Illegal to Buy Prop Money in Australia? The Plain-English Answer
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/is-it-illegal-to-buy-prop-money-australia/
- Published: 2026-10-05

Is it illegal to buy prop money in Australia? In most cases, no. Buying clearly marked reproduction notes for a film, a stage show, a photo shoot or a training exercise is a normal business purchase. What is illegal is making, using or passing off notes that could deceive someone into accepting them as real money. This guide separates the two, explains the situations where people get into trouble, and gives you a plain checklist. It is general information, not legal advice.

## The short answer

Buying prop money is lawful when the notes are clearly marked as reproductions, differ from genuine notes, and are bought for a legitimate purpose. The risk comes from what happens after the purchase: spending prop notes, presenting them as real, removing the markings or buying notes that were never marked in the first place. The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) is the law that applies, and Section 22 is the provision our compliance standard is built around.

## Buying, using and making are three different things

Most confusion comes from treating these as one question.

- Buying marked reproduction notes from a local supplier for production use is routine.
- Using them means handling them on set, in a studio or in a training room. That is lawful when the notes are marked, controlled and not offered as payment.
- Making reproductions yourself is where people fall into trouble, because a home-printed note that looks convincing has none of the safeguards a professional studio builds in. Do not make your own.

## What keeps a prop lawful

Three things carry most of the weight, and a supplier should be able to show you each of them.

1. It is marked. Every PROPPS note carries permanent specimen markings in line with Section 22 and the Reserve Bank's reproduction guidance.
2. It is different. Real Australian banknotes are polymer. Our reproductions are printed on non-reflective archival paper, so they are easy to tell apart by touch.
3. It is honestly sold. The product description states that the notes are non-legal tender props made for film, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training.

Read more about how this works in our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) and on our [compliance page](/compliance/).

## Situations that cause problems

The notes are rarely the problem. The situations around them are.

- Spending a prop note. Handing a prop note to a shop, a taxi driver or an ATM, even as a joke, is the fastest route to a police report.
- Pranks and stunts. A video of someone "paying" with prop cash can be treated as an attempt to deceive, whatever the caption says.
- Covering the markings. Removing, cropping or hiding the specimen markings changes the legal position of the notes.
- Buying unmarked notes. Notes with no markings, or with markings so faint they are easy to miss, are the main cause of trouble for buyers.
- Careless storage. Loose prop notes left in a car, a costume pocket or a rental can end up in the wrong hands.
- Cash giveaways. Content that suggests real cash is being given away, using prop notes, can mislead viewers and attract complaints.

## Shooting in public places

If your scene is shot in a street, shop or bank, tell the venue or local police beforehand and keep the supplier's invoice on set. Staff and members of the public cannot tell what is a prop from a distance. A short written note from the production company and a call to the local station can prevent a long afternoon.

Two further habits help. First, keep notes under the prop master's control and count them in and out each shooting day. Second, never let background performers keep souvenir notes. Even a single marked note in a wallet can turn into a question that nobody wants to answer.

## What if you are asked about a prop note?

Stay calm and show the markings. Explain that the note is a reproduction made for production use and show the supplier invoice. If you are speaking to police, it is reasonable to offer the supplier's details and the production file. Buying from a local, ABN-registered studio makes this simple. Overseas sellers on marketplace sites usually cannot supply any of it. For concerns about counterfeit currency, the [Australian Federal Police](https://www.afp.gov.au/) is the point of contact.

## Crossing borders with prop money

Carrying prop notes into or out of Australia raises extra questions. Customs officers see a bundle of banknote-like paper and have to decide what it is. Declare the notes, carry the invoice and keep the markings visible. If you are travelling for a shoot, ask the production's customs broker or legal adviser before you pack. Shipping from a local supplier with traceable dispatch is almost always simpler than carrying notes in luggage. Read about our [shipping and dispatch](/blog/shipping-and-dispatch-how-fast-can-you-get-prop-money-in-australia/) options.

## What insurers and location owners usually ask for

Insurers and location owners are not lawyers, and they rarely ask for legal analysis. They want to know three things: what the notes are, who supplied them and who is responsible for them. A short file covers all three:

- The supplier's invoice, with the business name, ABN and address.
- A photo of the front and back of a note, showing the specimen markings.
- A line in the call sheet or prop schedule naming the scene and the person in charge of the notes.

Bring the same file to any public location shoot. It turns a long conversation with a nervous venue manager into a short one.

## Common myths

"It is only illegal if you spend it." Spending is the clearest problem, but removing the markings, presenting prop cash as real or buying unmarked notes also create risk.

"Prop money is illegal everywhere." It is not. Marked reproductions are a normal supply item in the Australian film, theatre and photography industries.

"A home-printed note is cheaper and just as safe." It is neither. A home-printed copy has no specimen markings and no supplier paperwork, and a convincing copy is exactly what the law is written to catch.

## Why we publish this guide

PROPPS PTY LTD supplies prop currency to Australian productions, and the question we hear most often is whether the purchase itself is a problem. We would rather answer it plainly on a public page than leave buyers to guess from forum posts or from sellers who have a reason to say "no problem at all". If you read nothing else, remember the order of operations: buy marked notes from a supplier you can identify, keep the paperwork, control the notes on set and never offer them as payment.

## Is it illegal to buy play money or party money?

Buying play money, toy money or novelty party notes is not illegal. They are designed to look nothing like real currency. If you want something a little more realistic for a themed event, choose marked notes from a local supplier and keep them out of circulation. Our [novelty money guide](/blog/novelty-money-for-parties-and-events-whats-legal-in-australia/) and [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) suit that use.

## A practical checklist before you buy

1. Confirm the notes carry permanent specimen markings, and ask for a photo of the front and back.
2. Buy from an Australian business with an ABN and a physical address.
3. Check the notes are paper, not polymer.
4. Make sure the product page states the notes are non-legal tender props.
5. Choose signed-for delivery.
6. File the invoice and a note of the production use.
7. Brief everyone who will touch the notes: never spend them, show them off as real cash or post unmarked close-ups.

The term props money might sound like a simple toy, but in Australia, it is a highly regulated product. ### Can You Buy Prop Money in Australia? What You Can Order and What to Check
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/can-you-buy-prop-money-in-australia/
- Published: 2026-10-04

Can you buy prop money in Australia? Yes. Production companies, photographers, theatres, advertising agencies and training providers buy marked reproduction notes every week. The legal point is not whether you can buy them but what you are buying and what you do with it. This guide explains who buys prop money, what a legitimate order looks like, how to check a supplier, what it costs and how to place an order, in plain English. It is general information, not legal advice.

## The short answer

You can buy prop money in Australia from a local supplier when the notes are clearly marked as reproductions, differ from genuine notes in material and treatment, and are sold for legitimate purposes. You cannot use prop money as payment, and you should not buy notes that are marketed as spendable, undetectable or "real looking" with no markings. Our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/) explains the law behind that line.

## Who buys prop money

Prop money has a surprisingly wide customer base. The most common buyers are:

- Film and television productions: art departments dressing bank, casino, crime and street scenes.
- Theatre companies: stage cash that reads from the back row without needing to be genuine.
- Photographers and content studios: lifestyle, fashion and advertising shoots where cash is a visual element.
- Advertising and event agencies: branded prop currency for campaigns and launches.
- Training providers: cash-handling and security exercises where real money is not appropriate.
- Event organisers: parties, fundraisers and casino nights, where marked novelty notes are enough.

Different buyers need different things. A feature film needs hundreds of notes in realistic bundles. A party host needs a few marked stacks. Our [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) covers the five denominations used on screen, and our [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) suit lighter use.

## What a legitimate order looks like

A lawful order has four features, and you can check all four before you pay:

1. Visible specimen markings on every note. Ask for a photo of the front and back. The marking should be permanent and prominent, not a faint watermark.
2. A local supplier with an ABN. You can then see who you are paying, get an invoice and contact someone if there is a problem.
3. Paper, not polymer. Real Australian banknotes are polymer. Reproductions on matte paper are easy to tell apart by touch. PROPPS prints on non-reflective archival paper.
4. A clear use. The product page states what the notes are for: film, television, theatre, photography, art or training.

## How to check a prop money supplier

A few minutes of checking separates a studio you can rely on from an anonymous seller:

- Business details. Look for an ABN, a physical address and a working phone number. PROPPS PTY LTD is based in Eltham, Victoria, and has supplied Australian productions since 2019.
- Product descriptions. The copy should say the notes are non-legal tender props. Be wary of any listing that describes them as spendable or able to pass tests.
- Dispatch. Traceable shipping with a signature is a good sign. Offers of "discreet" or unmarked packaging are a bad one.
- Track record. Look for named productions, a physical studio, policies for returns and shipping, and a compliance page that quotes the law accurately.
- Overseas marketplaces. Listings that ship polymer notes copying current Australian designs sit close to the legal line and can be stopped at the border. Our guide to [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/) compares the options.

Prices vary with note count, denomination and how closely the finish matches the shot you need. Stack products are sized by face value, so you can scale from a single hero stack to a full bank vault.

A few rules of thumb:

- A single scene with one hero stack is usually covered by the minimum order.
- A bank or casino scene needs many bundles but only a few hero notes. Mix quantities to match what the camera sees.
- A season of a series costs less per scene when you order once, which is what our [wholesale page](/wholesale/) is for.

## How to order, step by step

1. Decide the use. Write down the scene, the denominations and roughly how many bundles are visible.
2. Pick the notes. Start with the [$100](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) and [$50](/shop/new-notes/50-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) products, which dominate Australian screen work, and add smaller denominations for tills and wallets.
3. Check the minimum and delivery threshold. Orders start at $300 AUD and delivery is free from $500 AUD.
4. Place the order. You can pay at checkout, including by crypto for the 10% discount.
5. Receive it. Orders are dispatched by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express with a mandatory signature on delivery, so make sure someone is at the delivery address.
6. File the paperwork. Keep the invoice and the specimen marking details with the production file.

## Choosing denominations and bundle sizes

Australian screen work leans on the $50 and $100 notes because their colours read strongly on camera, but a believable cash scene usually mixes denominations. Use $100 and $50 notes for hero stacks and close-ups. Add $20, $10 and $5 notes for tills, wallets and counter exchanges, where an all-$100 drawer would look wrong. Our guide to the [best Australian banknote denominations for film and TV](/blog/best-australian-banknote-denominations-for-film-and-tv-scenes/) shows how to split a budget across them.

Bundle size matters as much as denomination. The camera sees the top note and the edges of a stack, so a heavy-looking bundle does not always need a heavy order. Many art departments buy a handful of hero stacks and fill the rest of the frame with filler paper behind them. If you are unsure, [contact the studio](/contact/) with the shot list and we will suggest a quantity.

## Common mistakes when buying prop money

- Ordering from the cheapest listing. A low price often means no markings, no invoice and no one to call. Our guide to [cheap prop money](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) explains where the saving really goes.
- Leaving it to the last week. Express dispatch is fast, but a signature is required, so allow time to arrange someone at the delivery address.
- Forgetting storage. Decide who holds the notes between shooting days before they arrive.
- Skipping the paperwork. An invoice and the marking details take two minutes to file and answer most questions later.

## Buying for a one-off event versus a production

A one-off buyer, such as someone dressing a casino night or a photo shoot, usually needs a small order and no wholesale terms. A production company buying for a series needs consistency between orders, so the notes in episode six match the notes in episode one. If that is you, mention it when you [contact the studio](/contact/), because repeat orders can be planned and priced together. Either way, the legal checklist is the same: marked notes, an Australian supplier, an invoice and signed-for delivery.

## What you cannot do with prop money

Buying is lawful when the notes are marked and the purpose is legitimate. These are not:

- Spending prop notes, even once, as a test or a joke.
- Handing prop notes to anyone as a tip, a gift or a payment.
- Posting close-ups that suggest the cash is real.
- Removing or covering the specimen markings.
- Selling prop notes as genuine currency.

If a police officer or a shop assistant asks about a note, show the specimen marking and the invoice. That is what they are for. The [Australian Federal Police](https://www.afp.gov.au/) is the right contact for concerns about counterfeit currency, and the RBA publishes guidance on banknote reproductions.

### Prop Money Compliance Checklist: What Every Australian Production Must Know
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/prop-money-compliance-checklist-what-every-australian-production-must-know/
- Published: 2026-09-15

Legal and insurance sign-off on prop currency is a standard, non-negotiable step for most Australian productions — and it's far easier to satisfy upfront than to fix during a shoot. Here's the condensed checklist our studio recommends to every new production client.

1. Specimen markings present on both sides — every note should carry clear, indelible "SPECIMEN" or "REPRODUCTION" text, not a removable sticker.
2. Material and dimension deviation from genuine notes — confirmed by the supplier, not just visually assumed.
3. Supplier documentation on request — a legitimate Australian prop house should be able to confirm compliance with the [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) in writing for your production's legal file.
4. No marketing language claiming the props are "undetectable" or "spendable" — this framing itself signals non-compliant intent regardless of the physical product.
5. Local dispatch and ABN-registered supplier — simplifies invoicing, tax documentation, and any warranty or replacement claims.

### A Brief History of Australian Currency Notes for Set Designers
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/brief-history-of-australian-currency-notes-for-set-designers/
- Published: 2026-05-30

Getting the cash right in a period piece is a small detail that seasoned viewers notice immediately. Australia moved from pounds, shillings, and pence to decimal currency in February 1966 — any production set before that date should never feature dollar notes on screen, a mistake that shows up more often than it should in lower-budget period productions.

The [National Museum of Australia](https://www.nma.gov.au/) holds an extensive currency and social history collection worth reviewing if your production spans a specific decade — the note designs, paper stock colour, and even typography shifted noticeably across the 1970s, 80s, and the transition to polymer notes in the 1990s.

Our current [Film & TV Props](/shop/film-and-tv-props/) range is built around the modern polymer-era note designs. If your production is set in a specific historical period and needs a matching older design, mention it when you [contact our studio](/contact/) — we take custom period requests on a case-by-case basis.

### Fake Money vs Prop Money: Understanding the Legal Difference in Australia
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/fake-money-vs-prop-money-the-legal-difference-in-australia/
- Published: 2026-05-10

Search for "fake money" in Australia and you will find everything from board game tokens to listings that cross a legal line. The phrase covers too much ground to be useful, and the difference between lawful imitation money for a production and an offence under Commonwealth law is not a matter of taste. This guide explains the vocabulary, the tests that separate prop money from counterfeit currency, and the questions to ask before you buy. It is general information, not legal advice.

## Why the words matter

People use "fake money", "imitation money", "play money", "toy money", "prop money", "replica notes" and "counterfeit" as if they were interchangeable. They are not, and a supplier who uses them loosely is telling you something about how careful they are.

- Play money and toy money are obviously not real. They are brightly coloured, different in size and designed for games, classrooms and children. They carry almost no legal risk.
- Prop money is reproduction currency made for motion pictures, television, theatre, photography and training. It is designed to look right on camera while remaining clearly marked and clearly different in the hand.
- Imitation money is the broad everyday term for any of the above. On its own it tells you nothing about legality.
- Counterfeit currency is made or used to deceive. It is a criminal matter, and nothing in this article describes how to make it or where to get it.

## The legal line in one paragraph

The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) protects Australian currency. The law cares about whether an item could deceive a reasonable person into accepting it as genuine, and about what someone does with it. A reproduction with clear, permanent specimen markings, a different material and size or treatment, and honest marketing sits on the lawful side. A note made to pass at a till does not. Our [compliance page](/compliance/) explains how PROPPS builds to Section 22 and the Reserve Bank's reproduction guidance.

## Four tests that separate prop money from counterfeit

Use these four tests on any supplier, including us.

### 1. Is it marked?

Every note should carry permanent, prominent markings such as SPECIMEN or a statement that it is for motion picture use only. Markings that can be rubbed off, cropped out or hidden in fine print do not count. Ask for a photo of the note's front and back before you order.

### 2. Is it different from a genuine note?

Real Australian banknotes are printed on polymer and carry layered security features. A prop that is also polymer and copies every feature is not a prop in any sense that matters. PROPPS prints on non-reflective archival paper, which reads correctly on camera and feels different in the hand.

### 3. Is the marketing honest?

A legitimate seller describes the product as a prop, names the permitted uses and states that it is not legal tender. Warning signs include phrases about passing detection tests, "undetectable" quality, unmarked or discreet delivery, and unsourced claims of government clearance. Honest copy never suggests you can spend the product.

### 4. Is the intended use legitimate?

Film, television, theatre, advertising, photography, art and simulation training are all clear uses. A "prank" at a restaurant, a social media stunt that presents prop cash as real, or any attempt to pay for something is misuse, whatever the notes were bought for.

## Comparing the options

Here is how the common categories line up for a buyer:

- Board game and toy money: safe, but looks wrong on camera and is not made for production use. Our guide to [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) covers the choice.
- Marked prop currency from a local studio: the right choice for a scene that needs realism and a paper trail.
- Unmarked "realistic" notes from marketplace sellers: the highest risk. They may be held at the border, and a buyer who cannot show specimen markings has nothing to show a police officer or an insurer.
- Anything described as counterfeit or sold to be spent: illegal. Do not buy it.

## What this looks like on a real production

A drama set in a bank needs a few hundred $100 notes in the drawer and one hero stack on the counter. The art department orders marked notes from an Australian supplier, files the invoice, stores the notes with the prop master and counts them in and out each shooting day. When a location owner asks what the cash is, the answer is a one-page supplier statement and a note in the call sheet.

A photographer shooting a lifestyle campaign uses a fanned handful of $50 notes. The notes are marked, the shoot is in a studio, and nothing leaves the building. Compare that with a content creator who films themselves handing prop cash to strangers: the notes are identical, but the use is not.

Read more on the creator side in our [guide to prop money for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/) and our [photography guide](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/).

## Questions to ask before you buy

1. Are the notes marked, and can I see a photo of the markings?
2. Is the supplier an Australian business with an ABN and a physical address?
3. What material are the notes printed on?
4. How are they delivered, and is a signature required?
5. Does the seller state what the notes may and may not be used for?
6. Will I get an invoice and a written description I can put on the production file?

## Common myths

"If it is clearly a prop, nothing can go wrong." The markings protect you only when they are on the note and you can show them. A prop kept in a wallet, spent or posted as real cash loses the protection that the markings and the invoice give you.

"A disclaimer in the listing is enough." A line of small print on a website does not travel with the note. The marking has to be on the note itself, where anyone who picks it up can read it.

"Overseas notes are the same, only cheaper." They often are not. Polymer notes that copy current Australian designs closely are the category most likely to be stopped at the border, and you will have no local supplier to call if something goes wrong.

"Everyone knows it is a prop on a film set." The crew do. A bank teller, a shopkeeper or a passer-by watching a street shoot does not. Briefing the venue first is part of using prop money responsibly.

"Only big productions need to worry." The rules do not scale with budget. A student short and a feature film both need marked notes, a supplier invoice and a sensible plan for who holds the cash. Smaller crews often have less legal back-up, so a clean paper trail matters more, not less.

## Why we avoid the word "fake" on our product pages

Buyers do search for "fake money", and our guides use that phrase where it helps people find accurate information. But we do not describe products as fake, spendable or lookalike cash, because it frames the product as something it is not. Our notes are reproduction props. They are specimen-marked, they are paper rather than polymer, and they are made for the screen, the stage and the classroom.

Novelty cash for a bucks night, milestone birthday, or casino-themed party sits in a legal grey area in a lot of buyers' minds — but the rule is actually simple. Under the [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/), the same specimen-marking requirements apply whether the notes end up on a film set or scattered across a party table.

What this means practically for event planners:
- Confirm every note is clearly and permanently marked "SPECIMEN" or equivalent, not just a sticker that can be peeled off.

### How Much Prop Money Do You Need for a Scene? A Quantity Guide for Producers
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/
- Published: 2026-03-21

Under-ordering prop cash is one of the most common last-minute production scrambles — a duffel bag that reads as "half full" on a wide shot rarely fixes itself with clever framing. Before you place an order, work backwards from the shot list.

Rules of thumb our studio uses with production designers:
- Close-up counting scenes: 1–2 [strapped stacks](/shop/money-stacks/) is usually enough — the camera only ever sees the top and edges.
- Duffel bag or briefcase reveals: budget 10–20 stacks depending on bag size, since empty space reads immediately on camera.
- Vault or heist wide shots: 50+ stacks, often supplemented with background-only "filler" bundles that never get a close-up.
- Table-toss or "money rain" sequences: order in bulk and expect some wear — this is the one scenario where cheaper stock is actually the right call.

Our [bundle-size selector](/shop/new-notes/) scales from a Starter Stack right up to 100-Stack bulk orders, and organisations like [Ausfilm](https://ausfilm.com.au/) publish general Australian production-budgeting resources worth reviewing alongside your prop list if this is your first local shoot.

### Play Money vs Prop Money: Which One Do You Need?
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/
- Published: 2026-03-11

"Play money" and "prop money" get used interchangeably online, but they're built for different jobs. Board-game play money is a toy — thin card stock, cartoonish colours, sized for children's hands, and regulated under Australia's general toy and [product safety standards](https://www.productsafety.gov.au/) rather than currency law.

Prop money is closer to the genuine article in size, weight, and print detail, which is exactly why it needs the stricter specimen-marking treatment under the Crimes (Currency) Act rather than toy safety rules. If you're planning a kids' party game night, [play money style products](/shop/event-and-party-props/) with bold novelty branding are the right (and cheapest) choice. If you're shooting a close-up cash-counting scene, a photo booth backdrop, or an Instagram unboxing video where the cash needs to read as real on camera, you want cinema-grade [prop money for photography](/shop/photography-props/) instead.

Mixing the two up is the single most common mistake we see from first-time buyers — a stack of toy play money will not survive a macro lens the way archival-paper prop notes do.

### Where to Buy Prop Money in Australia (Legally)
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/where-to-buy-prop-money-in-australia-legally/
- Published: 2026-03-01

Search for "buy prop money Australia" and the results are a mixed bag: overseas marketplaces, unmarked novelty listings, forum posts and the occasional professional studio. Not all of it is lawful to import, carry or use on an Australian set. This guide explains where to buy prop money in Australia legally, how to compare your options, what to check before you pay and what a sensible order looks like. It is general information, not legal advice.

## The short answer

Buy marked, non-legal tender reproduction notes from an Australian business you can identify, with an ABN, a physical address, clear product descriptions and traceable delivery. That combination gives you an invoice for the production file, a local contact if something goes wrong and notes that are built to the standard in the Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) and the Reserve Bank's reproduction guidance. You can read the detail in our [Section 22 guide](/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/).

## Your five options for buying prop money

Most buyers end up choosing between these five routes. Each has a different risk profile.

### 1. A local prop currency studio

A specialist Australian studio is the best fit for film, television, theatre and advertising work. You get notes made for the screen, specimen markings on every note, an invoice, local support and Australia Post Express delivery. PROPPS PTY LTD works this way from Eltham, Victoria, and has supplied more than 500 Australian film, television and theatrical productions since 2019. Browse the [New Notes range](/shop/new-notes/) to see the product.

### 2. A general prop hire house

Some hire houses stock a few bundles of stage cash. This works for a single day of theatre, but selection is limited, notes may be reused and finishes vary. It is a reasonable fallback for tiny jobs, not a plan for a series.

### 3. Party and novelty shops

Novelty and party shops sell play money that looks nothing like real currency. That is safe and suits children's games, fundraisers and classrooms, but it will not hold up in a close-up. Our guide to [play money vs prop money](/blog/play-money-vs-prop-money-which-one-do-you-need/) explains where the line sits.

### 4. Overseas marketplaces

Overseas listings are where most trouble starts. Sellers often ship polymer notes that copy current Australian designs closely, with faint or no specimen markings, long delivery times and no one to contact. Parcels can be held at the border. Our comparison of [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/) goes through the differences in detail.

### 5. Making your own

Do not print your own. A home-printed copy has no safeguards, no markings and no paperwork, and a convincing copy is exactly what the law is written to catch.

## What to check before you buy

Spend five minutes on this checklist before you place an order with any seller.

1. Specimen markings. Every note should carry permanent, prominent markings. Ask for a close-up photo of the front and back of an actual note, not a render.
2. Material. Real Australian banknotes are polymer. Reproductions printed on matte paper are easy to tell apart by touch. PROPPS notes are printed double-sided on 120gsm archival paper.
3. Business details. Look for an ABN, a physical address and a working phone number. You should be able to say who you paid.
4. Honest descriptions. The product page should say the notes are non-legal tender props made for film, television, theatre, visual arts or training. Treat any claim of "government clearance", "undetectable" quality or "unmarked" delivery as a warning.
5. Delivery. Traceable shipping with a signature on delivery is the sensible standard. PROPPS ships by [Australia Post](https://auspost.com.au/) Express with a mandatory signature.
6. Policies. A real supplier publishes shipping, refund and privacy policies and a compliance page.
7. Paperwork. You should receive an invoice you can keep on the production file.

## Why local matters

Buying from an Australian studio changes a number of small things that add up on a production:

- Speed. Express dispatch from Melbourne takes days, not weeks. A late change to the call sheet is manageable.
- Recourse. If a parcel is damaged or a count is wrong, you can ring someone.
- Paperwork. A local invoice answers questions from insurers and location owners.
- Currency fit. A local studio keeps up with changes to the real note designs, so your on-screen cash looks current.
- Lower legal risk. Local specimen-marked notes avoid the border and compliance questions that come with overseas polymer copies.

## How much to expect to pay

Prices depend on denomination, bundle size and finish. At PROPPS, orders start at $300 AUD, delivery is free from $500 AUD and payments in cryptocurrency receive a 10% discount. Notes are sold in stacks, from a Starter Stack up to 100 Stacks for large scenes. For help matching quantity to the shot, read [how much prop money you need for a scene](/blog/how-much-prop-money-do-you-need-for-a-scene/). If you are watching the budget, our [cheap prop money guide](/blog/cheap-prop-money-what-you-are-really-paying-for/) explains where a low price usually comes from.

## A simple buying process

1. List the scenes. Write down which scenes show cash, which denominations are visible and whether any shot is a close-up.
2. Choose the denominations. Start with the [$100](/shop/new-notes/100-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) and [$50](/shop/new-notes/50-australian-prop-money-for-sale/) products, then add $20, $10 and $5 notes for tills and wallets.
3. Choose stack sizes. Match stack size to what the camera sees. Our guide to [$100 prop money bundle sizes](/blog/100-dollar-prop-money-which-bundle-size/) shows how.
4. Order early enough. Express dispatch is quick, but a signature is required, so plan who will be at the address.
5. File the paperwork. Keep the invoice and a note of the specimen markings with the production file.
6. Control the notes on set. Store them with the prop master and count them in and out each day.

## Buying for different uses

The right order depends on the job, and so does what you should ask the supplier.

- Film and television. You need volume, matching stacks and fast dispatch. Ask about wholesale rates if the order will repeat across a season, and keep the invoice with the production file.
- Theatre. Notes are seen from a distance, but they are handled backstage every night. Ask about durability and how many notes a run needs. Our [event and party props](/shop/event-and-party-props/) suit lighter stage use.
- Photography. Close-ups show print detail and paper finish. Matte stock avoids glare under strobes. See our [photography guide](/blog/prop-money-for-photography-realistic-cash-shots-without-the-risk/).
- Advertising and branded content. Agencies often want a branded or custom look. Our [custom and branded props](/shop/custom-and-branded-props/) cover that, and the legal checklist still applies.
- Training and simulation. Cash-handling trainers need notes they can reuse and account for. Keep them in the training room and record their return.
- Events and parties. Marked novelty notes are enough. Keep them out of circulation and away from shops and taxis.

## Warning signs in a listing

A few phrases tell you a listing is written for the wrong reason. Be cautious of copy that promises notes which pass detection tests, describes the product as "real looking" without mentioning markings, offers discreet or unmarked delivery as a feature, or claims government clearance without linking to a document. A professional studio describes what the product is, who it is for and how it is marked. It does not need to sound like a secret.

Be equally careful with listings that hide the seller. If there is no ABN, no address, no phone number and no policies, there is nobody to hold responsible when a parcel goes missing or a count is short. Those are the same details an insurer or location owner will want to see.

## What not to do after you buy

The law is mostly concerned with what happens after the purchase. Never spend prop notes, never hand them out as tips or gifts, never cover or crop the markings in publicity stills and never post unmarked close-ups that suggest the cash is real. If someone asks about a note, show the specimen markings and the invoice. Our guide to [whether it is illegal to buy prop money](/blog/is-it-illegal-to-buy-prop-money-australia/) goes through the common situations that cause problems, and the [Reserve Bank of Australia](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) publishes guidance on banknote reproductions.

### Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 & RBA Prop Money Rules Explained for Australian Filmmakers
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/crimes-currency-act-1981-rba-prop-money-guidelines/
- Published: 2026-02-15

If you are buying prop money for a shoot, a stage show or a training exercise, the law is the first thing your producer, insurer or legal team will ask about. This guide sets out the prop money Australia laws that matter in plain English, how the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) approaches reproductions of banknotes, and the practical steps an art department can take so the paperwork holds up. It is general information, not legal advice. For a specific production, check the current text of the legislation and speak to your own lawyer.

## The short answer

Making, using or passing off imitation currency as real money is a serious offence in Australia. Buying and using clearly marked reproduction notes for a legitimate production purpose is a normal part of screen, stage and photographic work. The difference comes down to four things: how the notes are marked, how they differ from genuine banknotes, how they are marketed, and what you do with them afterwards.

## What the Crimes (Currency) Act 1981 is aimed at

The Commonwealth [Crimes (Currency) Act 1981](https://www.legislation.gov.au/) sits alongside the Criminal Code and deals with offences relating to currency. Its purpose is to protect the integrity of Australian money. In practice that means it targets counterfeit currency, and reproductions that could realistically be accepted by a reasonable person as the real thing.

Section 22 is the provision our compliance standard is built around. In summary, it is concerned with making or possessing things that look like Australian currency without a lawful basis. A reproduction that is clearly and permanently marked, and that differs from a genuine note in ways a reasonable person would notice, is treated very differently from a note that has been made to deceive. Always read the current wording of the Act on the official legislation site, because amendments happen and a blog post is never a substitute for the text.

Two points are worth stating clearly:

- The offence is about deception and misuse, not about the existence of a prop. Film, television, theatre and photography have used reproduction currency for as long as those industries have existed.
- Intent matters, but intent alone is not a defence. A prop that looks identical to a real note and is carried in a wallet is a problem regardless of what the owner meant.

## What the RBA says about reproductions

The [Reserve Bank of Australia](https://www.rba.gov.au/banknotes/) is responsible for Australian banknotes and publishes guidance on reproducing banknote images. The guidance exists because banknotes carry security features, and because convincing copies cause real problems for shops, banks and the public. The RBA's position, in broad terms, is that reproductions must be clearly distinguishable from genuine notes, for example through changes in size, one-sided printing, or prominent markings, and must not be used in a way that could mislead.

The RBA updates its guidance when new banknote series are released, so check its banknote pages before you finalise a brief. If your production needs something the standard guidance does not cover, such as a close-up hero shot of a new-series note, the RBA is the body to ask, and the answer should go on your production file.

## How PROPPS builds notes to the standard

Every product PROPPS PTY LTD sells is a non-legal tender reproduction prop made solely for motion pictures, television, theatre, visual arts and simulation training. We have been supplying Australian productions from Eltham, Victoria since 2019, and more than 500 film, television and theatrical productions have used our work. The compliance standard behind every note is simple:

1. Specimen markings on every note. Each note carries permanent specimen markings so that no one could mistake it for legal tender at a glance or in the hand.
2. Paper, not polymer. Genuine Australian banknotes are printed on polymer. Our notes are printed on non-reflective archival paper, so the feel is different the moment someone picks one up.
3. Deliberate differences from a genuine note. We design reproductions to deviate from the real thing in material and treatment, not just in a label.
4. Honest marketing. We never describe prop notes as spendable, undetectable or interchangeable with real money. Our pages say what the product is and what it is for.
5. Traceable dispatch. Orders ship by Australia Post Express with a mandatory signature on delivery, so every parcel has a named recipient.

You can read the same standard on our [compliance page](/compliance/), which is the page to send to a producer or insurer who wants it in one place.

## A compliance checklist for productions

Use this list when you brief the art department or prepare a production file. It takes about ten minutes and answers most of the questions an insurer or location owner will raise.

1. Name the purpose of the notes in the call sheet or prop schedule, for example "reproduction currency for scene 14, bank counter".
2. Keep a copy of the supplier's invoice and the specimen marking details on the production file.
3. Store prop notes with the prop master or art department, not loose in a costume pocket or a personal bag.
4. Brief the cast and background performers: the notes are for the camera and they are never spent, shown off or posted as real cash.
5. If you shoot in a public place, tell the venue or local police beforehand, and keep a copy of the supplier details on set.
6. Return, destroy or securely store unused notes at wrap. Do not leave them in a location or hire car.
7. Keep close-up hero shots of any note under your own control and check the RBA's current guidance before you publish stills or trailers.

## Red flags when you choose a supplier

Prop currency is sold by a mix of professional studios and anonymous sellers. A few signals should make you stop and ask questions:

- Claims of "government clearance", "RBA approved" or "100% compliant" with no source. Regulators do not hand out approvals for individual prop sellers. If a claim has no link to a document, treat it as a sales line.
- Language about passing detection tests. Anything that suggests the notes could fool a pen, a scanner or a cashier is describing the wrong product.
- Discreet or unmarked shipping offered as a feature. Legitimate props do not need to hide. Traceable, signed-for delivery is the safer arrangement for everyone.
- No Australian business details. An ABN, a physical address and a contact number are the minimum. You should be able to confirm who you are paying.
- Overseas listings of polymer notes that closely copy current Australian notes. These sit much closer to the legal line and can be held up at the border.

For more on weighing up local and overseas options, see our guide to [local vs overseas prop money suppliers](/blog/local-vs-overseas-prop-money-suppliers-compared/).

## Using prop money on set and in public

Most compliance problems happen after the camera stops, not in the shot. A few habits prevent them:

- Do not hand prop notes to anyone outside the production, including as a joke or a tip.
- Do not use them at a shop, ATM, taxi or vending machine, even as a test.
- Do not post unmarked close-ups to social media with captions implying the cash is real.
- Do not leave notes visible in a parked car on location.
- If a member of the public or an officer asks, show the specimen markings and the supplier invoice. That is what they are for.

## Special cases

Content creators and advertising. The same rules apply to a social media video as to a feature film. If the clip is meant to look like a real cash giveaway, the risk is the presentation, not the prop. Read our guide to [prop money for content creators](/blog/prop-money-for-content-creators-social-media-and-photoshoot-guidelines/).

Training and simulation. Banks, retailers and security trainers use reproduction notes for cash-handling exercises. Keep the notes in the training room and record their return.

Theatre. Stage use is low risk because the audience is at a distance, but backstage handling still needs control. Our [theatre-friendly range](/shop/event-and-party-props/) is built for that.

### How Cinematographers Light Prop Money on Camera to Eliminate Glare
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/lighting-prop-money-for-camera-avoiding-glare/
- Published: 2026-01-20

Shooting prop money under bright studio lighting presents unique optical challenges. Real polymer [Australian banknotes](https://www.rba.gov.au/) reflect high-output LED panels and Fresnel fixtures, creating blown-out specular highlights that ruin close-up focus.

PROPPS PTY LTD engineered our cinema series prop notes specifically to overcome this obstacle. Our 120gsm matte finish absorbs harsh incident light while maintaining vivid saturation for the emerald greens of the $100 and the rich ochre gold of the $50.

DP Pro Tips:
- Use soft, diffused side lighting (cross-key) rather than direct top-down lighting to highlight note texture without glare.
- Incorporate subtle back-rim lighting to define the edges of strapped bundles against dark mahogany desks or metal vault surfaces.
- In high-speed slow-motion shots (120fps+), our matte paper maintains crisp micro-contrast as notes flutter through the air.

### The Art Department Guide: Weathering Prop Cash for Underworld Realism
- URL: https://proppsptyltd.com.au/blog/art-department-guide-weathering-prop-cash/
- Published: 2025-11-10

Pristine, crisp banknotes right out of the wrapper can immediately pull viewers out of a gritty crime thriller or street-level drama. Genuine circulated cash is softened, creased, and carries subtle patina from countless human transactions.

To achieve organic aging:
- Mechanical Tumbling: Run stacks through clean cloth tumblers or gently crumple and re-flatten individual notes by hand.
- Coffee & Tea Washes: Dilute instant dark roast coffee to create a warm, non-toxic staining wash applied with a soft atomizer spray.
- Edge Burnishing: Lightly drag graphite or fine charcoal along the edges of the bundle to simulate years of friction in wallets and cash drawers.

PROPPS PTY LTD also offers pre-distressed bundles prepared by professional Melbourne scenic artists, saving your art department dozens of prep hours. Industry bodies like [Screen Australia](https://www.screenaustralia.gov.au/) publish broader art department resources worth reviewing alongside your prop list.
